                                               VisRes Bench: On Evaluating the Visual Reasoning Capabilities of VLMs

                                                                   Abstract                                    In contrast, VLMs, despite excelling at captioning and
                                                                                                           visual question answering, fail at these fundamental tasks
                                            Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have achieved remark-            when linguistic guidance is removed, unable to reconstruct
                                         able progress across tasks such as visual question answer-        partially visible components or maintain spatial continu-
                                         ing and image captioning. Yet, the extent to which these          ity [25]. These perceptual deficits cascade into higher-level
                                         models perform visual reasoning as opposed to relying on          reasoning failures [48]. Without textual input, VLMs strug-
                                         linguistic priors remains unclear. To address this, we intro-     gle with compositional reasoning and even simple attribute-
                                         duce VisRes Bench, a benchmark designed to study visual           based relations, with performance collapsing on multi-
                                         reasoning in naturalistic settings without contextual lan-        attribute tasks [21]. Text-conditioned competence does not
                                         guage supervision. Analyzing model behavior across three          transfer to purely visual benchmarks, revealing that appar-
                                         levels of complexity, we uncover clear limitations in per-        ent reasoning capabilities may reflect linguistic priors rather
                                         ceptual and relational visual reasoning capacities. VisRes        than genuine visual understanding.
                                         isolates distinct reasoning abilities across its levels. Level        Findings from cognitive neuroscience indicate that
                                         1 probes perceptual completion and global image matching          relational reasoning develops along a graded percep-
                                         under perturbations such as blur, texture changes, occlu-         tual–conceptual continuum, where early visual representa-
                                         sion, and rotation; Level 2 tests rule-based inference over       tions support increasingly abstract relational and composi-
                                         a single attribute (e.g., color, count, orientation); and Level   tional inference [3, 14]. This continuum progresses hier-
                                         3 targets compositional reasoning that requires integrating       archically: perceptual grounding (recovering object prop-
                                         multiple visual attributes. Across more than 19,000 con-          erties from visual input) supports single-attribute reason-
                                         trolled task images, we find that state-of-the-art VLMs per-      ing (e.g., tracking color or count transformations), which
                                         form near random under subtle perceptual perturbations,           in turn enables multi-attribute composition (e.g., reasoning
                                         revealing limited abstraction beyond pattern recognition.         jointly over color, count, and spatial relations). Because
                                         We conclude by discussing how VisRes provides a unified           these stages build on one another, failures in perceptual
                                         framework for advancing abstract visual reasoning in mul-         extraction propagate upward: models that cannot form re-
                                         timodal research.                                                 liable visual representations cannot perform rule-based or
                                                                                                           compositional reasoning over them. Current VLMs exhibit
                                                                                                           fragile generalization under perceptual variation, highlight-
                                         1. Introduction                                                   ing the need for benchmarks that jointly evaluate perceptual
                                                                                                           and reasoning stages and diagnose where visual processing
                                         Humans reliably complete partial visual information, re-          breaks down [17, 24].
                                         constructing occluded objects, continuing interrupted pat-
                                         terns, and inferring abstract rules from spatial arrange-            We introduce VisRes, a benchmark that spans this pro-
                                         ments. This ability draws on multiple levels of visual pro-       gression from perceptual grounding to structured visual rea-
                                         cessing—from perceptual organization via Gestalt princi-          soning in real-world imagery. The three levels of Vis-
                                         ples [38] and amodal completion [27, 35] to attribute recog-      Res operationalize increasing reasoning demands: percep-
                                         nition and compositional reasoning—supporting stable ob-          tual reconstruction (recovering structure under occlusion
                                         ject identity, spatial continuity, and causal understanding.      and degradation), single-attribute rule abstraction (infer-

                                                                      four-choice visual selection format. As shown in Figure 1,
                                                                      Level 1 assesses perceptual grounding through local patch
                                                                      completion and global scene reconstruction under visual
                                                                      degradation. Level 2 (5,956 samples across 12 subtasks)
                                                                      evaluates rule inference over a single visual attribute 3×3
                                                                      using Raven-style grids. Level 3 (2,522 samples across 6
                                                                      subtasks) requires multi-attribute compositional reasoning,
                                                                      with grids governed by concurrent rules spanning multiple
                                                                      visual domains. Together, these levels provide a structured
                                                                      framework for diagnosing visual reasoning capabilities in
                                                                      current models.

                                                                      3.1. Task Design and Taxonomy
                                                                      Perceptual Completion Tasks: Includes local patch com-
                                                                      pletion and global occlusion. Local tasks match a masked
                                                                      tile to one of four candidates under controlled perturbations
                                                                      (blur, brightness, rotation, edges, orientation), while global
                                                                      tasks require inferring scene structure when 50–80% of the
                                                                      image is occluded. These tasks assess the robustness of low-
Figure 2. Illustrative pattern rules used in Levels 2 and 3 tasks.
                                                                      level visual representations under degradation.
Top: Level-2 tasks where one attribute varies across the row. Bot-    Single-Attribute Rule Tasks: These use a 3×3 Raven-
tom: Level-3 tasks where multiple attributes vary. See Section 3.3.   style grid where the missing cell is determined by a row-
                                                                      wise rule applied to one attribute—color, count, or orien-
                                                                      tation—while others vary freely. Rules include progres-
studying visual reasoning under tightly controlled settings,          sions, categorical distributions (3-different or 2-similar–1-
but have limited transfer to real-world imagery. More nat-            different), and simple arithmetic operations, enabling tar-
uralistic reasoning tasks—including Bongard-OpenWorld                 geted evaluation of single-attribute abstraction.
[41], Bongard-HOI [18], and V-PROM [34] have advanced                 Multi-Attribute Rules: These tasks require integrating
relational reasoning in realistic imagery and helped moti-            multiple jointly varying attributes such as color, count, ob-
vate our design, but typically operate within a single do-            ject identity, and orientation. Subtasks span coupled rules,
main and lack level-structured tasks. VisuLogic [43] and              independent multi-attribute rules, and spatially structured
VERIFY [6] focus on synthetic, diagram-based quantita-                patterns like spirals, probing whether models can compose
tive and spatial reasoning, while VISFACTOR [15] probes               several transformations simultaneously, reflecting the high-
fundamental visual cognition using psychometric-inspired              est level of relational and compositional difficulty in Vis-
subtests. These benchmarks extend reasoning evaluation                Res. The detailed taxonomy is provided in the supplemen-
in controlled settings, but typically rely on synthetic stim-         tary, expanding the one given in Table 1 and Section 3.3.
uli and do not structure tasks across perceptual, single-
attribute, and multi-attribute level.                                 3.2. Image Collection and Preprocessing

patches are extracted from non-overlapping regions of the                                           ence of a rule applied to a single target attribute while oth-
same image without intersecting the masked tile. In DS,                                             ers vary freely. The missing cell is fixed at position (2,2)

pled, DINOv2-large embeddings are computed, and the                                                 effects. The logical structures within rows include:

Level-1: Models exhibit consistent performance patterns
across perceptual transformations. Rotation achieves higher       To establish an upper bound, we recruited five human
accuracy across models (35.42% GPT-5, 37.5% Qwen3-4B,             participants who each completed 200 tasks sampled from
36.05% Qwen3-30B, 34.38% Gemini), suggesting that ori-            across the benchmark, including 20 tasks from each of

                Question: You are presented with a main image in which a square region is blanked out (occluded).

                Below the image are four candidate patches labeled A, B, C, and D, arranged horizontally from left to right.

                Exactly one patch correctly restores the missing region of the main image.

                Task: 1. Focus on local visual cues around the blank area — such as color, texture, object edges, and
                lighting direction; 2. Compare these clues with each candidate patch to determine which one best aligns
                structurally and contextually with the main image; 3. Select the patch that fits seamlessly into the blank
                region, maintaining spatial alignment and structural consistency with the surrounding image.

                In your reply, follow this format exactly:

                Reasoning: Describe the main rule or pattern and explain briefly why your answer fits it.

                Answer: [A, B, C, or D]














                                                                GPT-5-Thinking

                                                                Reasoning: The blank area covers the yellow house facade
                                                                above the horizontal dark gutter band, with red roof tiles
                                                                above and the diagonal capped wall crossing the bottom
                                                                edge. Patch C shows this mix—yellow wall (no dormer), red
                                                                tiles at the top, a bit of greenery on the left, and the
                                                                horizontal dark band—matching the surrounding edges and
                                                                textures. The other patches either include a dormer (D), a
                                                                roof corner/wall that doesn’t align (B), or a window and
                                                                layout that don’t match (A).

                                                                Model Answer: C  



                         Ground Truth: A ✓

                Perceptual failure: correctly identifies some visual features but places them in the wrong location;
                overrelies on visible cues and fails to reason about missing structures (e.g., window on correct patch A),
                resulting in incorrect alignment.

                 structural and spatial cues — how edges, object boundaries, lighting, and geometry align between the
                 patch and the surrounding region; 3. Select the patch that matches the occluded area when correctly
                 oriented, maintaining overall continuity and coherence with the main image.

                 In your reply, follow this format exactly:

                 Reasoning: Describe the main rule or pattern and explain why your answer fits it.

                 Answer: [A, B, C, or D]














                                                                GPT-5-Thinking

                                                                places the window in the right position, matching the wall

Question: You are presented with a main image in which a square region is blanked out (occluded).

Below the image are four candidate patches labeled A, B, C, and D, arranged horizontally from left to right.

Exactly one patch correctly restores the missing region of the main image.

Task: 1. Focus on local visual cues around the blank area — such as color, texture, object edges, and
lighting direction; 2. Compare these clues with each candidate patch to determine which one best aligns
structurally and contextually with the main image; 3. Select the patch that fits seamlessly into the blank
region, maintaining spatial alignment and structural consistency with the surrounding image.

In your reply, follow this format exactly:

Reasoning: Describe the main rule or pattern and explain briefly why your answer fits it.

Answer: [A, B, C, or D]















                                             GPT-5-Thinking

                                             Reasoning: To the left of the blank square we see the bird’s
                                             gray neck, and to the right is the green background. The
                                             correct patch must continue this left-to-right transition
                                             (gray bird on the left edge, green background on the right)
                                             without including features like the beak or eye. Patch D
                                             matches this orientation and texture, while A shows an eye,
                                             B has green on the left, and C contains the beak.

                                             Model Answer: D✓




          Ground Truth: D✓

Perceptual success: the model successfully grounds the visible cues (neck-to-background transition)
and selects the correct patch with consistent spatial continuity.

Question: You are presented with one main image in which a substantial part of the scene is occluded or
masked. Alongside it, you are shown four complete candidate images, labeled A, B, C, and D.

Exactly one candidate represents the original, unoccluded version of the main image.

Task: 1. Focus on the visible structures and contextual cues within the occluded image — such as object
outlines, edges, colors, textures, and spatial layout; 2. Compare these visible regions with each of the four
candidates to determine which one aligns most closely in terms of composition, geometry, and contextual
meaning; 3. Choose the candidate that best matches the occluded image and restores the original scene.

In your reply, follow this format exactly:

Reasoning: Describe the main rule or pattern and explain why your answer fits it.

Answer: [A, B, C, or D]













                                                GPT-5-Thinking

                                                Reasoning: The occluded image shows a brick house with a
                                                white arched doorway, a white car in its driveway, and a
                                                neighboring tan house with a hedge and black car to the
                                                right. The left neighboring house is clearly visible.
                                                Candidate B matches this composition and perspective
                                                best—the amount of the left house shown, the alignment of
                                                the cars/hedge, and the street view all line up. A shows less
                                                of the left house, while C and D are taken from farther right.

                                                Model Answer: B  





Ground Truth: A✓            B                   C                    D

Perceptual failure: the model relies on coarse semantic similarity (houses, cars, street) but misjudges the
exact viewpoint and spatial layout.

                                         Level 2 - Orientation Uniform




Question: You are presented with a visual reasoning puzzle consisting of a 3×3 grid of images with one
image missing in the bottom-right corner of the grid.

Below the grid are four candidate options, labeled A, B, C, and D, arranged horizontally from left to right.

Exactly one option correctly completes the grid.

Task: 1. The logical relationship between images is defined within each row, and the same rule or
transformation pattern applies consistently across all rows in the grid. 2. Study the grid and observe how
the orientation or direction of elements varies, alternates, or rotates within each row.

3. Identify the option that best continues this orientation rule and correctly completes the grid.

In your reply, follow this format exactly:

Reasoning: Describe the main rule or pattern and explain why your answer fits it.

Answer: [A, B, C, or D]


















                                               GPT-5-Thinking

                                               Reasoning: Within each row, the orientation alternates: a
                                               side view followed by a front view, then a back view. 
                                               Row 3 currently has a side view (green car) and a front view
                                               (high chair), so the missing image must be a back view.
                                               Among the options, only A clearly shows the back of an
                                               item (the cap’s back with the strap), while the others show
                                               front or flat views. 



                                               Model Answer: A




             Ground Truth: B✓



Orientation failure: the model cannot consistently judge object facing directions, so it infers a wrong
orientation rule and picks A instead of the uniformly oriented B.

                                         Level 2 - Count Arithmetic


Question: You are presented with a visual reasoning puzzle consisting of a 3×3 grid of images with one
image missing in the bottom-right corner of the grid.

Below the grid are four candidate options, labeled A, B, C, and D, arranged horizontally from left to right.

Exactly one option correctly completes the grid.

Task: 1. The logical relationship between images is defined within each row, and the same rule or
transformation pattern applies consistently across all rows in the grid; 2. Study the grid and observe how
the number of elements changes, repeats, or follows a progression within each row; 3. Identify the option
that best continues this numerical rule and correctly completes the grid.

In your reply, follow this format exactly:

Reasoning: Describe the main rule or pattern and explain why your answer fits it.

Answer: [A, B, C, or D]
















                                                GPT-5-Thinking

                                                Reasoning:Across each row, the number of items increases
                                                by one from left to right, and each row starts one higher
                                                than the row above it:

                                                   Row 1: 1 → 2 → 3

                                                   Row 2: 2 → 3 → 4

                                                   Row 3: 3 → 4 → 5 (missing).

                                                Among the options, D is the only one that represents five
                                                items in the square (five green tiles), so it completes the
                                                3,4,5 progression in the last row.
 

                                                Wrong reasoning with correct answer

                                                Model Answer: D ✓


           Ground Truth: D✓

Rule misidentification (count): the model guesses the correct option by matching an approximate 1–2–3 /
3–4–5 progression, but fails to detect the true within-row addition rule and miscounts the elements on
some images within the grid.

Question: You are presented with a visual reasoning puzzle consisting of a 3×3 grid of images with one
image missing in the bottom-right corner of the grid.

Below the grid are four candidate options, labeled A, B, C, and D, arranged horizontally from left to right.

Exactly one option correctly completes the grid.

Task: 1. The logical relationship between images is defined within each row, and the same rule or
transformation pattern applies consistently across all rows in the grid.; 2. Study the grid and observe how
colors change, repeat, or contrast within each row.; 3. Identify the option that best fits this color-based
rule and correctly completes the grid.

In your reply, follow this format exactly:

Reasoning: Describe the main rule or pattern and explain briefly why your answer fits it.

Answer: [A, B, C, or D]















                                               GPT-5-Thinking

                                               Reasoning: Each row cycles the dominant object color in
                                               the same order: Row 1 = brown → white → red; Row 2 =
                                               white → red → brown; therefore Row 3 must be red →
                                               brown → white. The missing image (row 3, col 3) should be
                                               predominantly white. Among the options, only A (the
                                               mushrooms) is mainly white.

                                                Model Answer: A ✓




                                                GPT-4o

                                                Reasoning: In each row of the grid, the images follow a
                                                specific color progression involving the colors brown, white,
                                                and red. In the first row, the sequence moves from brown
                                                (chair) to white (T-shirt) to red (shoebox). The second row
                                                continues this pattern but in a shifted order: white
           Ground Truth: A✓                     (umbrellas) to red (bucket) to brown (basket). In the third
                                                row, the first image is red (protractors) and the second is
                                                brown (wooden board), so the missing third image should
                                                be white to maintain the consistent cyclical color pattern.
                                                Among the answer choices, only Option A (mushrooms)
                                                predominantly features the color white, which completes
                                                the pattern logically.

                                                Model Answer: A ✓




Color reasoning success: both models correctly identify the cyclical color pattern across rows and
selects the patch that continues the distribution rule.




  Figure A.9. Level-2 Color Distribution (3-different): Prompt and Model Response Example
                                          Level 3 - Coupled Color-Count


Question: You are presented with a visual reasoning puzzle consisting of a 3×3 grid of images, where one image is
missing in one of the nine positions.

Below the grid are four candidate options labeled A, B, C, and D, arranged horizontally from left to right.

Exactly one option correctly completes the grid.

Task: 1. The grid follows a uniform logical rule, which governs the relationships between the images across the entire
grid; 2. In this puzzle, focus on the following attributes: number of elements (count) and color, which may vary
independently or in relation to one another; 3. Carefully analyze how the attributes vary in each image and across the
grid to infer the common rule that governs them; 4. Choose the option that best follows this rule and completes the grid
in a logically consistent way.

In your reply, follow this format exactly:

Reasoning: Describe the main rule or pattern and explain why your answer fits it.

Answer: [A, B, C, or D]

















                                                     GPT-5-Thinking

                                                     Reasoning: Count the number of items in each picture. 
                                                     Row 1 totals 3 + 4 + 1 = 8 items. 
                                                     Row 2 totals 6 + 2 + 1 = 9 items. 
                                                     Thus, the rule is that the total number of objects per row
                                                     increases by 1 each row, so Row 3 must total 10. The
                                                     existing images in Row 3 have 3 and 2 items, so the missing
                                                     cell must contain 5 items (10 − (3 + 2) = 5). Among the
                                                     options, only D shows five objects, and it also matches the
                                                     warm-color tendency of the first column.
 

                                                     Wrong reasoning with correct answer

                                                     Model Answer: D ✓


             Ground Truth: D✓

Coupled rule failure: the model ignores the count–color coupling and instead uses a row-sum heuristic
(“8, 9, 10”) plus a vague warm-color bias, arriving at the correct option D for the wrong reasons.




       Figure A.10. Level-3 Coupled Color-Count: Prompt and Model Response Example
                                         Level 3 - Independent Count-Object-Color



Question: You are presented with a visual reasoning puzzle consisting of a 3×3 grid of images, where one
image is missing in one of the nine positions.

Below the grid are four candidate options labeled A, B, C, and D, arranged horizontally from left to right.

Exactly one option correctly completes the grid.

Task: 1. The grid follows a row-wise logical rule, where multiple visual attributes change systematically
across each row; 2. The same rule or transformation pattern applies consistently across all rows in the
grid; 3. In this puzzle, focus on the following attributes: color, number of elements (count), and object
type, which may vary independently or in relation to one another; 4. Carefully analyze how these
attributes vary across each row, identify the common rule of change, and determine how it applies to the
row with the missing image; 5. Choose the option that best satisfies the row rule and completes the grid
in a logically consistent way.

In your reply, follow this format exactly:

Reasoning: Describe the main rule or pattern and explain why your answer fits it.

Answer: [A, B, C, or D]

















                                                       GPT-5-Thinking

                                                       Reasoning: Across each row, two things change in a
                                                       consistent way: the images move from a lighter color on the
                                                       left toward a darker color on the right, and the number of
                                                       items tends to decrease from left to right. 
                                                       Row 1 goes from white (stacked trays) → red/white (train
                                                       set) → red (single caboose). 
                                                       Row 2 goes from lighter metal/wood (three hammers) →
                                                       metal/wood (single hammer) → dark black (two vases). 
                                                       In Row 3 we already have a light image on the left (two
                                                       white planes) and a dark image on the right (black toaster).
                                                       The missing center image should therefore be mid-tone/red
                                                       and contain multiple (but not many) elements—between
                                                       the left’s two items and the right’s single item. Option C (the
                     Ground Truth: B✓                  red two-bin container) fits: it’s red (mid-tone) and shows a
                                                       small multiple, matching the row’s progression in both color
                                                       and count.

                                                       Model Answer: C



Compositional rule failure: the model misses the true row-wise rules for count (subtraction), color and
object identity (two-similar, one-different), and instead relies on vague heuristics (“lighter-to-darker,”
“decreasing count”), failing to integrate the attributes.




Figure A.11. Level-3 Independent Count-Object-Color: Prompt and Model Response Example
                                             Level 3 - Spiral Color-Count-Object




Question: You are presented with a visual reasoning puzzle consisting of a 3×3 grid of images, where one

image is missing in one of the nine positions.


Below the grid are four candidate options labeled A, B, C, and D, arranged horizontally from left to right.


Exactly one option correctly completes the grid.


Task: 1. The grid follows a spiral logical rule, where the visual attributes of the images form a continuous

sequence that progresses inward through the grid; 2. The spiral may move clockwise or

counterclockwise, and its starting position can vary anywhere within the grid; 3. In this puzzle, focus on

the following attributes: object type, color, and number of elements (count), which may vary

independently or in relation to one another; 4. Carefully analyze how each attribute varies along the spiral

path and determine how the rules interact to produce the overall pattern; 5. Choose the option that best

satisfies all relevant rules and completes the missing position in a logically consistent way.


In your reply, follow this format exactly:


Reasoning: Describe the main rule or pattern and explain why your answer fits it.


Answer: [A, B, C, or D]






















                                                          GPT-5-Thinking


                                                          Reasoning: Read the grid in a clockwise spiral starting from

                                                          the top-left cell (the missing one). 

                                                          Along this spiral, each object type repeats after four steps

                                                          with a different color, and the count for the repeated item

                                                          matches its earlier occurrence:


                                                             Bowls: 4 white (1,2) → later 3 green (3,2) — different

                                                             colors, same object.


                                                             Notes: 4 brown (1,3) → later 4 white (center).


                                                             Mugs: 1 red (2,1) → later 1 orange (2,3).


                                                             Socks: 2 red (3,3) → the first position of the spiral must

                                                             therefore be 2 socks in a different color.


                                                          Thus the missing image must be a pair of socks (count =

                                                          2) in a color different from red. Option C shows a pair

                          Ground Truth: C✓                of green socks, satisfying the spiral pairing rule (object type

                                                          repeats with a different color and matching count).




                                                          Model Answer: C ✓






Object Repetition Shortcut: the model selects the correct answer but does not follow the spiral traversal. 

Instead, it uses a shortcut: detecting repeated objects diagonally and choosing a new color with matching

count — bypassing the actual compositional rule.




       Figure A.12. Level-3 Spiral Color-Count-Object: Prompt and Model Response Example
                                      Level 3 - Spiral Color-Orientation


Question: You are presented with a visual reasoning puzzle consisting of a 3×3 grid of images, where one
image is missing in one of the nine positions.

Below the grid are four candidate options labeled A, B, C, and D, arranged horizontally from left to right.

Exactly one option correctly completes the grid.

Task: 1. The grid follows a spiral logical rule, where the visual attributes of the images form a continuous
sequence that progresses inward through the grid; 2. The spiral may move clockwise or
counterclockwise, and its starting position can vary anywhere within the grid; 3. In this puzzle, focus on
the following attributes: orientation and color, which may vary independently or in relation to one another;

4. Carefully analyze how each attribute varies along the spiral path and determine how the rules interact
to produce the overall pattern; 5. Choose the option that best satisfies all relevant rules and completes
the missing position in a logically consistent way.

In your reply, follow this format exactly:

Reasoning: Describe the main rule or pattern and explain why your answer fits it.

Answer: [A, B, C, or D]


















                                                 GPT-5-Thinking

                                                 Reasoning: Follow the clockwise spiral starting at the top-
                                                 left (cap) → beanie → orange mug → blue cap → wallet →
                                                 right-facing slide → white mug → [missing] → blue bicycle
                                                 (center). 
                                                 Two attributes change along the spiral:

                                                     Color cycles Neutral → Neutral → Warm → Cool → Warm
                                                     → Neutral → Neutral → Warm → Cool. 
                                                     So the missing image must be warm-colored.

                                                     Orientation alternates whenever the object has a
                                                     direction (mugs/footwear/teapot/bike): right (orange
                                                     mug) → right (slide) → left (white mug) → left (missing)
                                                     → right (bike). 
                                                     Thus the missing image should face left.

                                                 Option A, the brown teapot, is warm-colored and faces left
            Ground Truth: C✓                     (spout to the left), fitting both spiral rules; the other options
                                                 don’t satisfy both constraints.

                                                 Model Answer: A


Spiral and orientation failure: although the model initially tracks the correct color sequence, it drifts into a
vague warm/cool categorization and misreads orientation cues, ultimately picking A (with matching color
but wrong orientation) instead of following the true spiral rule.
